Bad: No active antivirus is registered. Turn Windows Defender back on: Settings > Privacy & security > Windows Security > Virus & threat protection.

Normal: Antivirus definitions are stale. Open the product and run its update, or check its subscription state.

Bad: Real-time protection is OFF — files are only checked when manually scanned. Re-enable it in Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Manage settings.
If you didn't turn it off yourself, treat that as a red flag: malware often disables protection first. Run a full scan.

Normal: Defender definitions are a few days old — open Windows Security and check for protection updates.
Bad: Definitions are over a week old; scans miss current threats. Update in Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Protection updates.

Normal: Tamper protection is off — malware can silently disable Defender. Turn it on in Windows Security > Virus & threat protection settings.
Review the exclusion list (Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Manage settings > Exclusions) and remove anything you don't recognize — hiding in an exclusion is a classic malware trick.
Bad: An unusually large number of scan exclusions is configured. Review every one; malware routinely excludes its own folders from scanning.
The firewall is off for this profile. Re-enable it: Windows Security > Firewall & network protection.
UAC is disabled — any program can gain admin rights silently. Re-enable it: search 'UAC' in Start and set the slider to the default level.

Normal: UAC prompts are not shown on the secure desktop, which makes them spoofable. Restore the default UAC level.

Bad: SmartScreen is off — you lose the warning before running unrecognized downloads. Re-enable it in Windows Security > App & browser control.
Normal: SmartScreen state is unrecognized on this build — verify it in Windows Security > App & browser control.

Bad: The Winlogon Shell/Userinit values are non-standard — a well-known malware persistence point. Run a full antivirus scan immediately.
If a scan finds nothing, research the exact value shown in the details before restoring the default (some corporate tools legitimately modify it).

Normal: Some startup programs have no publisher signature. That alone is not malware — many small tools are unsigned — but make sure you recognize each one listed in the details.
Unknown items: disable them in Task Manager > Startup apps first (reversible), then scan the file in Windows Security.

Bad: A startup item's digital signature FAILS verification — the file may have been tampered with. Do not ignore this.
Disable the item in Task Manager > Startup apps and run a full antivirus scan now.
